gbs333-aa7264-d1e107.summary: States the question, whether only an operation of a sensitive power is praxis, and explains that it is raised to clarify the following questions on practical and speculative knowledge. Biel notes that Ockham recites and rejects two opinions, the second being Scotus's (Prologue q. 5): praxis is an act of a power other than the intellect, naturally posterior to intellection, apt to be elicited in conformity with right reason so as to be right. He refers to Ockham's fuller treatment in I d. 35 q. 6 and in the second book (q. 3), whose understanding is needed here.
claims: The question on praxis is posed to clarify the following questions on practical knowledge.
Scotus defines praxis as an act of a power other than the intellect, naturally posterior to intellection, apt to be elicited in conformity with right reason; Ockham rejects this.
The matter is more fully resolved in Ockham's I d. 35 q. 6.

gbs333-aa7264-d1e157.summary: Second consideration: the question is more about a name than a thing. In reality our actions unfold in a fixed sequence: the intellect shows the end and the means; volition of the end follows or can follow; then counsel about the means, a judgment dictating what to choose and omit, choice, and, if nothing impedes, execution. The question is only which of these should be called praxis.
claims: The question of what praxis is is primarily verbal, not real.
Human action proceeds through: intellectual presentation of end and means, volition of the end, counsel, judgment, choice, and execution.

gbs333-aa7264-d1e187.summary: Sets out Eustratius's four senses of praxis: (1) broadly, any operation of any power, free or natural; (2) strictly, any cognitive operation or a passion following on cognition, so that every act of a cognitive or appetitive power and passions like delight and sorrow are energeia or praxis; (3) more strictly, an operation within our power, such as every work of virtue or vice; (4) most strictly, an operation elicited in conformity with the dictate of right reason and the choice of the will. The question concerns only the third or fourth sense.
claims: Eustratius distinguishes four increasingly strict senses of praxis.
Only the third (an operation within our power) and fourth (an operation conforming to right reason and choice) senses are relevant here.

gbs333-aa7264-d1e226.summary: Explains that the distinction between practical, speculative, and counseling (consiliativus) intellect is one of names, not things, since the same intellect is all three. The practical intellect holds practical principles or conclusions, such as a dictate that some end is to be sought (the end in action being like a principle in speculative matters, since the will acts only for an end dictated by reason or freely set by itself). The counseling intellect concerns only practical conclusions about means: given an end, it inquires and concludes by what means it is best attained. The practical intellect is therefore superior to and broader than the counseling intellect, since it covers both ends and means. The speculative intellect considers things not in our power.
claims: Practical, speculative, and counseling intellect are distinguished by name, not as distinct things.
The end in practical matters functions as a principle does in speculative ones.
Every non-final act of the will presupposes a volition of the end.
The counseling intellect concerns only means; the practical intellect concerns both ends and means and so is superior.
The speculative intellect considers what is not in our power.

gbs333-aa7264-d1e317.summary: On the third sense of praxis, every operation in our power, whether volition, intellection, sensation, or external operation, is praxis. But since volition is primarily in our power and other acts only through volition, praxis is said primarily of the will's act and secondarily of others (cf. d. 35 q. 6). Every act in our power can be virtuous or vicious, as it conforms or not to right reason, so praxis divides into virtuous and vicious. Virtuous praxis is defined as an operation in the power of our will, apt to be elicited in conformity with right reason so as to be right. The 'in the power of the will' clause excludes natural operations, which are neither praised nor blamed; the 'conforming to right reason' clause excludes vicious praxis, which is elicited in conformity with erroneous reason.
claims: In the third sense, every operation in our power, whether volition, intellection, sensation, or external action, is praxis.
Praxis is predicated primarily of acts of will and secondarily of other acts.
Praxis divides into virtuous and vicious.
Virtuous praxis is an operation in the will's power, apt to be elicited in conformity with right reason.
Natural operations are not praxis, since in involuntary acts we are neither praised nor blamed.

gbs333-aa7264-d1e395.summary: First corollary: not every praxis has a practical science to which it ought to conform. Vicious praxis, such as hatred of enemies against the divine precept, cannot be elicited in conformity with right reason.
claims: Not every praxis has a corresponding practical science.
Vicious praxis cannot conform to right reason.

gbs333-aa7264-d1e411.summary: Second corollary: some praxis is elicited neither in conformity nor in disconformity with right reason, e.g. a volition following the intellect's mere presentation of an object without any prior true or false dictate.
claims: Some praxis is neither conformed nor contrary to right reason, such as volition after bare presentation of an object without dictate.

gbs333-aa7264-d1e424.summary: Third corollary: pure speculation can be praxis, since it can be in the will's power and be commanded and elicited by it, both as an end and as a means, e.g. when the intellect dictates study for the sake of beatitude, holiness, or recreation, and it can be meritorious or demeritorious. Yet practical knowledge is not therefore speculative knowledge, as will appear.
claims: Pure speculation can be praxis when it is commanded by the will.
Speculation can be meritorious or demeritorious.
This does not make practical knowledge identical with speculative knowledge.

gbs333-aa7264-d1e454.summary: Fourth corollary: praxis does not signify an act alone but an act connoting the will as freely and effectively producing it, as with a meritorious act. In the fourth sense, praxis signifies an act of will eliciting or commanding after the intellect's counsel, and so concerns only means, not ends, since, as Aristotle says in Ethics III, we deliberate not about ends but about means (the doctor does not deliberate whether to heal). Still, an operation that is an end can be called praxis in this sense insofar as it can be ordered by prior counsel to a further end.
claims: Praxis is a connotative term: it signifies an act while connoting the will freely producing it.
In the fourth sense, praxis is an act of will following counsel and concerns means only.
We deliberate about means, not ends (Aristotle).
An act that is an end can still be praxis insofar as it is ordered to a further end through counsel.

gbs333-aa7264-d1e511.summary: Responsive conclusion: not only the operation of a sensitive power is praxis; every operation of will, intellect, sense, and external movement that lies in the will's power is truly praxis in the third or fourth sense, because each can be virtuous or vicious.
claims: Not only sensitive operations are praxis.
Every operation of will, intellect, sense, or external motion in the will's power is praxis.

gbs333-aa7264-d1e529.summary: First corollary to the conclusion: every act of the will is praxis, both elicited and commanded acts, the elicited primarily and the commanded through it. An elicited act (willing or nilling) belongs to the will as such; a commanded act is an act of another power (intellect, sense, motive power) caused or conserved by the will's command.
claims: Every act of the will is praxis.
Elicited acts (velle, nolle) are primarily praxis; commanded acts are praxis through elicited acts.
Commanded acts are acts of other powers caused or conserved at the will's command.

gbs333-aa7264-d1e562.summary: Second corollary: every act of intellect, sense, and external motive power can be praxis, since it can fall under the will's command, unlike purely natural acts such as nutrition. 'Can' because an act that precedes the will, like the first intellection presenting an object to the will or a sensation prior to intellection, is not praxis as such, but becomes praxis if continued by the will's command, ordered to an end, or accepted or loved by the will.
claims: Any act of intellect, sense, or external motion can be praxis.
Purely natural acts such as nutrition cannot be praxis.
Acts preceding the will are not praxis unless continued, ordered, or accepted by the will.

gbs333-aa7264-d1e593.summary: Third corollary: an act that is not praxis can become praxis, and conversely. Example of the latter: an act caused by the will eliciting or commanding it, but afterwards conserved by God alone, ceases to be praxis.
claims: An act can begin or cease to be praxis.
An act conserved by God alone, not by the will, is no longer praxis.

gbs333-aa7264-d1e611.summary: Fourth corollary: every speculation can be praxis, so praxis and speculation are not really distinct. 'Speculation' can mean any act of understanding generally, or more strictly an act of understanding that does not direct some praxis.
claims: Every speculation can be praxis.
Praxis and speculation are not really distinct.
Speculation is either any act of understanding or, strictly, one not directive of praxis.

gbs333-aa7264.summary: Quaestio 10, raised to clarify the following questions on practical and speculative knowledge, asks whether only the operation of a sensitive power is praxis. Following Ockham against Scotus's definition of praxis as an act of a non-intellective power posterior to intellection, Biel treats the question as largely verbal: the real sequence of action (cognition of end and means, volition, counsel, judgment, choice, execution) is fixed, and the question is only which stage to call praxis. Of Eustratius's four senses of praxis, the third (any operation in our power) and fourth (an act of will following counsel, concerning means) are relevant. After distinguishing practical, speculative, and counseling intellect as names for one intellect, he argues that praxis is said primarily of acts of will and secondarily of other acts in the will's power, divides into virtuous and vicious, and is a connotative term implying free voluntary production. The conclusion is that every voluntary operation of will, intellect, sense, or external motion is praxis, and corollaries draw out the consequences. Every act of will is praxis, elicited acts primarily and commanded acts through them. Acts of other powers can become praxis, and stop being praxis, according to their relation to the will. Even pure speculation can be praxis, so praxis and speculation are not really distinct.
claims: Not only sensitive operations but every operation lying in the will's power, of will, intellect, sense, or external motion, is praxis.
Praxis belongs primarily to acts of the will and secondarily to acts commanded by it.
Praxis is a connotative term signifying an act together with the will freely producing it; hence an act may become or cease to be praxis.
Praxis and speculation are not really distinct; pure speculation can be praxis.
